| [LIT-156](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-156.md) v4 | An Emerging Dilemma for Reciprocal Causation | Hazelwood (2023), DOI-10.1017/psa.2023.124. Hazelwood defines RC as "the process of natural selection is both a cause and effect of processes such as niche construction" and EC as "natural selection is an emergent causal process". He argues they are incompatible. Emergence here is Wilson's synchronic dependence plus autonomy, cashed out as Pence's composition. If EC holds, niche construction partly composes selection, so the two fail Woodward's independent-fixability condition and cannot stand in a causal relation. If EC fails, selection is either non-causal (statisticalism) or individual-level, which is incoherent because relative fitness needs a population (Millstein, Sober). A reproducee is a B that comes after A, is caused by A, and is of A's relevant class. A reproducer is a reproducee with reproductive autonomy, meaning it can reproduce across a range of backgrounds. A Darwinian individual is a reproducer with high reproductive causal control, meaning heredity survives as the parent's description is made finer. On that vocabulary, genes of multicellular organisms are, like hearts, mere reproducees, but with high control. Material overlap is necessary for reproducers, which are whole life cycles, and unnecessary for reproducees, so Griesemer and Godfrey-Smith partly talk past each other. The ecological niche is the conditions that permit continued existence; for a population, mean absolute fitness ≥ 1. | [LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md) | Life as we know it | Friston (2013), J. R. Soc. Interface 10(86):20130475. Any ergodic random dynamical system whose states split into internal, sensory, active and external sets with a Markov blanket has internal and active states whose flow can be written as a gradient descent on a variational free energy of the blanket and internal states (Lemma 2.1, Eqs. 2.5–2.8). They therefore "appear" to do Bayesian inference about external states and to bound their own entropy. A simulated "primordial soup" of 128 coupled Lorenz subsystems forms a blanket-enclosed cluster whose internal states predict external motion (5 of 82 above a time-reversed null) and which disperses when blanket or internal states are lesioned. The paper says a candle flame cannot have a Markov blanket, and concedes that the universe holds countless blankets, conjecturing that minimum-entropy blankets mark life. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-421](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-421.md)), from the published text (the author's posted PDF of the journal version and the PMC full text). Worth reading as the founding statement of the Markov-blanket formulation of the free energy principle applied to life, and as the one text in the record that names a candle flame and says it is not lifelike. Read it as a redescription, not a derivation: its "heuristic proof" shows that the flow of an ergodic system with a Markov blanket can be written as a gradient flow on a variational free energy, by choosing the variational density to equal the posterior. The free energy is variational, not thermodynamic; no heat or entropy production is computed. The simulation is one run, analysed with a blanket chosen by spectral clustering. |

Worth reading as the canonical statement of the "gradient-dissipation" view of life: living systems and ecosystems are dissipative structures that develop so as to degrade the solar gradient more completely, and the second law is "a necessary but not sufficient cause for life". Read the thermodynamics as a programme, not a derivation. The "restated second law" is offered as a corollary of Kestin's stability result but not derived from it. The ecological evidence is one stressed-versus-control marsh pair and a few thermal-scanner and satellite comparisons, all correlational. It draws no line between living and non-living dissipative structures beyond "memory" (DNA). |
| [LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md) | Biological Autonomy: A Philosophical and Theoretical Enquiry | Moreno & Mossio (2015), Springer, History, Philosophy and Theory of the Life Sciences 12. The book argues that biology should revolve around autonomy, not only natural selection: organisms are organized systems that self-produce and self-maintain as integrated wholes, set their own goals and norms, and promote the conditions of their existence through interaction with their environment. Chapters treat constraints and organisational closure, emergence and inter-level causation, teleology and function, agency, evolution, organisms and levels of autonomy, and cognition. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the chapter list. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read. The book is not open access at Springer, but the authors deposited a copy of it in HAL (hal-01151449, "Book_Autonomy_web.pdf", CC BY-NC 4.0, deposited 13 May 2015). HAL now serves files behind an anti-bot challenge that requires a browser running JavaScript, and it states that the challenge is there against automated scrapers, so I did not try to get past it. A human reader can open the copy lawfully, and a reading from it would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-566](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-566.md) | Defining Agency: Individuality, Normativity, Asymmetry, and Spatio-temporality in Action | Barandiaran, Di Paolo & Rohde (2009), Adaptive Behavior 17(5):367–386. Three conditions are jointly necessary and sufficient for minimal agency: the system defines its own individuality, it is the active source of modulations of its coupling with the environment (interactional asymmetry), and it regulates that coupling by norms it generates (normativity). Generatively, an agent is an open autonomous system (a precarious network of mutually enabling processes) that adaptively modulates its coupling so as to maintain some of its constituent processes. Minimal life satisfies this; life is sufficient for agency but not necessary. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-458](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-458.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the standard organizational definition of minimal agency, and as the clearest statement that an agent is not the same thing as an individual. Individuality is one of three conditions, with interactional asymmetry and normativity; it is a precondition for the other two and is not sufficient for agency. The generative definition: an agent is an autonomous organization that adaptively regulates its coupling with its environment and contributes to sustaining itself as a consequence. The paper rejects statistical and energetic measures of asymmetry as sufficient, and says systems optimising an externally fixed function should not be treated as models of agency. |
| [LIT-570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-570.md) | An Organizational Account of Biological Functions | Mossio, Saborido & Moreno (2009), BJPS 60(4):813–841. A trait has a function iff it contributes to the maintenance of a self-maintaining organization, is produced and maintained under that organization's constraints, and the organization is differentiated. Closure grounds teleology and normativity in the current system, unifying etiological and dispositional accounts. Flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes have closure but no functions, because each makes a single undifferentiated contribution to its own maintenance. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-444](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-444.md)), from the HAL deposit of the submitted version. Worth reading as the organizational account of function and as the place where the organizational school says plainly that a candle flame has closure. Functions are contributions to a differentiated self-maintaining organization by traits that organization produces and maintains. Closure alone grounds teleology and norms but is shared by flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes; organizational differentiation is what functions need. Reproduction is admitted to be a problem and left to a sketch. |
| [LIT-582](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-582.md) | Biological organisation as closure of constraints | Montévil & Mossio (2015), J. Theor. Biol. 372:179–191. Two causal regimes act in organisms: processes (thermodynamic changes) and constraints, which act on processes while being conserved at the relevant time scale. Closure is mutual dependence among constraints: each is produced by a process another constraint constrains, and each helps produce another. Closure mixes slow and fast dependence, grounds functions, and is proposed as a boundary criterion. A volume-sweeping count of dependencies, the tendency to closure, separates symbionts that share an encompassing closure, and separated nested closures mark levels of organisation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-468](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-468.md)), from the authors' HAL deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the paper statement of the central claim of Biological Autonomy ([LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md)): biological organisation is closure of constraints. A constraint is defined by a symmetry: it acts on a process at a time scale at which it is itself conserved. Closure is a set of constraints each of which depends directly on another in the set and generates another, and cannot be split into two closed sets. The paper offers closure as a boundary criterion and gives a preliminary measure, the tendency to closure, for drawing boundaries between interacting organisms. It does not claim closure defines an organism. |
| [LIT-709](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-709.md) | Conceptualization of the Holobiont Paradigm as It Pertains to Corals | Goulet, Erill, Ascunce, Finley & Javan (2020), Frontiers in Physiology 11:566968, a review. A coral is a consortium: the animal plus the Symbiodiniaceae, bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses in its body, mucus and skeleton, and neighbours are excluded by definition. Membership can change, so one colony may be a different holobiont at different times. Traits such as thermal tolerance belong to the host–symbiont combination: not every Durusdinium is heat tolerant, and a novel anemone–alga pairing gave higher oxygen flux under heat than both natural ones. Measuring both partners shows different routes to the same bleaching outcome. Whether the holobiont is the unit of selection is asked, not answered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-555](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-555.md)); worth reading as a short, explicit statement of why a coral should be studied as a composite of host and microbes rather than as an animal with passengers. It is a mini-review with no data of its own (about 3,700 words), and its strongest point is conceptual: traits such as thermal tolerance belong to host–symbiont combinations, not to either partner. The physiological evidence it cites is thin and partly not from corals: its one demonstration that a combination is "not necessarily the sum of its parts" is an oxygen-flux experiment in the sea anemone Exaiptasia. It poses, and does not answer, whether the coral holobiont is a unit of selection. |
| [LIT-721](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-721.md) | Multilevel Selection and the Major Transitions in Evolution | Okasha (2005), Philosophy of Science 72:1013–1025. On how multilevel selection bears on the major transitions in evolution. Unread: the 2022 overview [LIT-749](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-749.md) cites it for the two levels at which selection can act during a transition and for the point that the traditional debate set aside the origin of the biological hierarchy. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. PhilSci-Archive, which holds the author's preprint, refused every request and was not bypassed; the journal copy is paywalled; a course copy on an instructor's personal domain was found and not used. Okasha's 2022 overview "The Major Transitions in Evolution—A Philosophy-of-Science Perspective" ([LIT-749](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-749.md)), read in full, cites it for the two-level view of transitions and restates its point that the traditional levels-of-selection debate set aside the origin of the hierarchy. Filed because it is the paper usually cited for multilevel selection in the major transitions. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-740](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-740.md) | Cancer across the tree of life: cooperation and cheating in multicellularity | Aktipis et al. (2015), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 370:20140219. Multicellularity rests on five kinds of cellular cooperation, and cancer is cheating on them. Surveying cancer-like growth across the independent origins of complex multicellularity, the authors find division-of-labour cheating in every form, and resource and environment cheating so far only in animals and plants. Complex multicellularity is a cheater detection and suppression system. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-562](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-562.md)): in full, from the open-access deposit in PubMed Central (CC BY 4.0). Worth reading as a survey of cancer-like growth across the independent origins of multicellularity, read as cheating on five foundations of cooperation: proliferation inhibition, controlled cell death, division of labour, resource allocation and maintenance of the extracellular environment. Cheating on division of labour is reported in every form of multicellularity, and complex multicellularity is described as a cheater detection and suppression system. Limits: a literature review with no model or new data; absences may reflect lack of study, and animals' apparent susceptibility may reflect sampling. |
| [LIT-749](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-749.md) | The Major Transitions in Evolution—A Philosophy-of-Science Perspective | Okasha (2022), Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 10:793824. A major transition is the evolution of a higher-level unit from formerly free-living units. For one to succeed, higher-level selection must trump selection within the collective, typically through policing or aligned interests. The transitions turn the biological hierarchy from explanans into explanandum, vindicate multi-level selection, and leave the highest occupied level privileged as that of organisms. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-586](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-586.md)): in full, from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY). Worth reading as a philosopher's map of the major evolutionary transitions. A transition is the evolution of a higher-level unit from formerly free-living ones; for it to succeed, selection between collectives must come to trump selection within them, typically through policing, kinship or division of labour. The transitions make the biological hierarchy something to be explained rather than assumed, and leave the highest occupied level privileged as the level of organisms. Limits: a review with no model or data, provisional by its own account; it cautions that general principles may explain each transition only coarsely. It stands in for the unread 2005 paper [LIT-721](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-721.md). |
| [LIT-817](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-817.md) | On the Normal and the Pathological | Canguilhem (1943; expanded 1966; English 1978, reissued 1989), DOI-10.1007/978-94-009-9853-7. Against the nineteenth-century view that disease is a quantitative deviation from a normal state, it argues that the normal is normative: health is an organism's capacity to institute new norms in a changed environment, and disease a narrowed capacity to do so.
